'''Theodore Hsu''' {{Postnom|MPP}} (pronounced "shoe": [[Traditional Chinese characters|Chinese]]: 徐正陶; born March 4, 1964) is a Canadian physicist and politician who has represented [[Kingston and the Islands (provincial electoral district)|Kingston and the Islands]] in the [[Legislative Assembly of Ontario]] since 2022 as a member of the [[Ontario Liberal Party]]. Before entering provincial politics, Hsu served as a [[Member of Parliament (Canada)|Member of Parliament]] (MP) representing [[Kingston and the Islands (federal electoral district)|Kingston and the Islands]] federally from the 2011 to 2015 as a member of the [[Liberal Party of Canada]]. On May 28, 2023, Hsu announced his candidacy for the [[2023 Ontario Liberal Party leadership election|2023 Ontario Liberal Party Leadership Election]] in which he was eliminated on the first ballot.<ref>{{Cite web |last=CBC News |date=May 28, 2023 |title=Kingston MPP Ted Hsu announces bid to lead Ontario Liberals |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/ontario-liberals-ted-hsu-kingston-1.6857124 |website=CBC News}}</ref>

== Early life and career ==
Hsu was born in [[Bartlesville]], [[Oklahoma]], in 1964 to James and Marjorie and is the oldest of three siblings. Hsu is of [[Chinese people|Chinese]] descent and is fluent in English, [[French language|French]], and [[Mandarin Chinese|Mandarin]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gerard|first=Steve|date=June 6, 2011|title=CBC: Ted Hsu, the Future of the Liberal Party?|work=Kingston Herald|url=https://kingstonherald.com/news/ted-hsu-future-of-liberal-party-201035173|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> When he was six months old, the family moved to Kingston, Ontario,<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ibbitson|first=John|date=May 10, 2011|title=Physicist, financial consultant, green advocate, father - and new Liberal MP|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/physicist-financial-consultant-green-advocate-father---and-new-liberal-mp/article579482/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> where his father joined [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] as a chemical engineering professor.

Hsu attended high school at Kingston's [[Loyalist Collegiate and Vocational Institute]]. In 1984, he graduated from [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]] with a Bachelor of Science Honours in physics. He pursued graduate studies at [[Princeton University]], where he completed his PhD in physics in 1989 after successfully defending his dissertation titled "Towards an understanding of the large U-[[Hubbard model]] and a theory for [[High-temperature superconductivity|high temperature superconductors]],"<ref>{{Cite book|last=Hsu|first=Theodore Cheng-Tao|date=1989|title=Towards an understanding of the large U-Hubbard model and a theory for high temperature superconductors|url=https://catalog.princeton.edu/catalog/995320853506421|access-date=February 21, 2022|website=Princeton University Library}}</ref> under the supervision of [[Philip W. Anderson]], recipient of the 1977 [[Nobel Prize in Physics]]. Hsu went on to complete post-doctoral research in [[Chalk River Laboratories|Chalk River]], [[Vancouver]], and [[France]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ibbitson|first=John|date=May 10, 2011|title=Physicist, financial consultant, green advocate, father - and new Liberal MP|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/physicist-financial-consultant-green-advocate-father---and-new-liberal-mp/article579482/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref>

Applying his technical and research skills in math, computing, and problem-solving to capital markets, Hsu worked as a researcher and trader in [[Paris]] and [[Philadelphia]] for [[BNP Paribas|Banque Nationale de Paris]], and as an executive director in the [[Tokyo]] office of [[Morgan Stanley]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=Physics Careers: Ted Hsu|url=https://careers.cap.ca/profile/hsu.html|access-date=February 21, 2022|website=Canadian Association of Physicists}}</ref>

Hsu is a long-term member of SWITCH, a Kingston-based [[Nonprofit organization|not-for-profit]] association that promotes local job creation and green economic growth. From 2007 to 2011, he served as the executive director of SWITCH<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gerard|first=Steve|date=June 10, 2011|title=CBC: Ted Hsu, the Future of the Liberal Party?|work=Kingston Herald|url=https://kingstonherald.com/news/ted-hsu-future-of-liberal-party-201035173|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> and compiled the first Greenhouse Gas Inventory for Kingston.

==Politics==
Hsu acted as treasurer of the Kingston and the Islands Federal Liberal Association from 2007 to 2010, and was an active member of its policy committee.<ref>{{Cite web|date=August 30, 2011|title=About Ted Hsu|url=http://tedhsu.liberal.ca/about_ted/ |url-status=deviated |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110830153457/http://tedhsu.liberal.ca/about_ted/ |archive-date=30 August 2011}}</ref> During this time, he supported the 2007 provincial and 2008 federal Liberal campaigns for [[John Gerretsen]] and [[Peter Milliken]], the longest-serving Speaker in the House of Commons.  Following Milliken's announcement in summer 2010 that he would not seek re-election, Hsu won the Liberal nomination in November to be the party's 2011 candidate.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gerard|first=Steve|date=July 6, 2010|title=Ted Hsu Launches Campaign to Replace Peter Milliken|work=Kingston Herald|url=https://kingstonherald.com/news/ted-hsu-launches-campaign-to-replace-peter-milliken-201031262|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|last=Clancy|first=Clare|date=November 9, 2010|title=If the Hsu fits, nominate it|url=https://www.queensjournal.ca/story/2010-11-09/news/if-hsu-fits-nominate-it/}}</ref>

=== In Parliament ===
In the federal election held on May 2, 2011, Hsu defeated [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative]] candidate Alicia Gordon by less than 3,000 votes. He was one of only two new Liberal MPs elected in Canada<ref>{{Cite news|last=Ibbitson|first=John|date=May 10, 2011|title=Physicist, financial consultant, green advocate, father - and new Liberal MP|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/physicist-financial-consultant-green-advocate-father---and-new-liberal-mp/article579482/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> in what was the [[2011 Canadian federal election|party's poorest showing in history]].

One of only a few MPs with an academic science background, Hsu served in the [[Liberal Party Shadow Cabinet of the 41st Parliament of Canada|Liberal Party shadow cabinet]] as the critic for science and technology. He also would serve as critic for the [[Federal Economic Development Agency for Southern Ontario]] and critic for the [[Federal Economic Development Initiative for Northern Ontario]].<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gerard|first=Steve|date=June 2, 2011|title=Kingston's Ted Hsu Receives Two Liberal Portfolios|work=Kingston Herald|url=https://kingstonherald.com/news/kingston-mp-ted-hsu-receives-two-liberal-party-portfolios-201035047|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> In August, 2013, Liberal leader [[Justin Trudeau]] appointed Hsu to an additional role as Liberal critic for post-secondary education.

In 2011, Hsu was the first runner-up to [[Conservative Party of Canada|Conservative]] MP [[Chris Alexander (politician)|Chris Alexander]] as Rookie of the Year, in ''[[Maclean's]]'' annual Parliamentarians of the Year awards.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Gerard|first=Steve|date=November 22, 2011|title=Kingston MP Ted Hsu Voted 1st Runner Up, Rookie of the Year|work=Kingston Herald|url=https://kingstonherald.com/news/ted-hsu-rookie-mp-award-201037253|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> Hsu was also the first runner-up for the Rising Star award for Maclean's in 2012<ref>{{Cite news|date=November 21, 2012|title=2012 Parliamentarians of the Year|work=Maclean's|url=https://www.macleans.ca/politics/ottawa/drumroll-please-the-2012-parliamentarians-of-the-year/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> and the annual accolades continued in November 2013, with Hsu winning the ''Maclean's'' Parliamentarian of the Year Award. He was voted by parliamentarians from all parties as the MP who "Best Represents Constituents."<ref name=":0">{{Cite web |date=November 18, 2013 |title=2013 Parliamentarians of the Year |url=https://www.macleans.ca/news/canada/presenting-the-2013-parliamentarians-of-the-year/ |access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref>

In August 2014, Hsu announced that he would not run for re-election in the upcoming 2015 federal election, citing the burdens of political life on his young family.<ref>{{Cite news|last=LeBlanc|first=Daniel|date=August 7, 2014|title=Rookie Liberal MP Ted Hsu won't run for re-election citing family balance|work=The Globe and Mail|url=https://www.theglobeandmail.com/news/politics/rookie-liberal-mp-ted-hsu-wont-run-for-re-election/article19948867/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref>

Before leaving federal politics, he introduced a noteworthy private member's bill in September 2014. "Bill C-626, An Act to Amend the Statistics Act"<ref>{{Cite web|date=2014|title=An Act to amend the Statistics Act (appointment of Chief Statistician and long-form census)|url=https://openparliament.ca/bills/41-2/C-626/?tab=mentions|access-date=February 21, 2022|website=Openparliament.ca}}</ref> was designed to appoint a [[Chief Statistician of Canada|chief statistician]] and to reinstate the long-form census, which had been eliminated by the Conservative Party in 2010.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Bede Scharper|first=Stephen|date=February 1, 2015|title=Why Canada should reinstate long-form census: Scharper|work=Toronto Star|url=https://www.thestar.com/opinion/commentary/2015/02/01/why-canada-should-reinstate-long-form-census-scharper.html|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> Ultimately, the long-form census was restored in 2015, immediately after the new [[2015 Canadian federal election|Liberal government took office]], but after Hsu had left (see [[Canada 2011 Census]].). Hsu also spent much of his time advocating for the return of the [[Prison farm|Canadian Prison Farm System]] which was re-instated, albeit in a more limited format, in 2019.

=== Post-Parliament ===
Upon leaving the House of Commons, Hsu served as the campaign manager for Liberal MPP [[Sophie Kiwala]] during the 2018 provincial election in Ontario and, in 2019, during the [[2019 Canadian federal election|Canadian federal election]] Hsu also managed the successful re-election campaign of [[Mark Gerretsen]], the Liberal MP who replaced him.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pinkerton |first=Charlie |date=2022-06-16 |title=Ted Hsu's back and considering an Ontario Liberal leadership run |url=https://www.qpbriefing.com/2022/06/16/ted-hsus-back-and-considering-an-ontario-liberal-leadership-run/ |access-date=2022-06-18 |website=QP Briefing |language=en-US}}</ref>

In 2017, Hsu joined SYNG pharmaceuticals, a Kingston-based biotechnology startup focusing on diagnosing and treating [[endometriosis]]. As an advisor for SYNG, Hsu provided communications support.

From 2019 to 2020, Hsu was asked to co-chair the Mayor's Task Force on Housing,<ref>{{Cite news|date=July 10, 2019|title=Want to move to Kingston? You may have trouble finding a home|work=CBC News|url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/ottawa/kingston-housing-shortage-move-1.5205699|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> which culminated in a report and a series of recommendations to address Kingston's challenging housing shortage.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2020|title=A Foundation for the Public Good|url=https://www.cityofkingston.ca/documents/10180/33838002/MTFH_Recommendation_Report_2020_2_26.pdf/94f30134-cd0d-161a-117f-317e73efc513?t=1582817514977|access-date=February 21, 2022|website=City of Kingston}}</ref>

=== Return to politics and Ontario Liberal leadership campaign ===
In 2020, Hsu announced his campaign to represent Kingston and the Islands as the [[Ontario Liberal Party]] candidate in the upcoming provincial election.<ref>{{Cite news|last=Mazur|first=Alexandra|date=July 30, 2020|title=Former MP announces bid for Liberal MPP nomination in Kingston and the Islands|work=Global News|url=https://globalnews.ca/news/7234263/ted-hsu-liberal-nomination-kingston-islands/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> He won the bid over previous MPP [[Sophie Kiwala]], who lost in the [[2018 Ontario general election|2018 Ontario election]], in November 2020.<ref>{{Cite web|date=November 7, 2020|title=Liberals in Kingston and the Islands Nominate Ted Hsu as 2022 Ontario Liberal Party Candidate|url=https://ontarioliberal.ca/liberals-in-kingston-and-the-islands-nominate-ted-hsu-as-2022-ontario-liberal-party-candidate/|access-date=February 21, 2022|website=Liberal Ontario}}</ref>

When asked about his motivations for re-entering politics, Hsu said, "As my kids and their young friends have grown up and become aware of their world, they tell me how worried they are." He went on to say, "I want to offer voters someone who has a proven record representing constituents, and also has experience working with scientists, climate researchers, economists, engineers and entrepreneurs."<ref>{{Cite news|last=Vilela|first=Cris|date=November 7, 2020|title=Ted Hsu wins provincial Liberal nomination for Kingston and the Islands|work=Kingstonist|url=https://www.kingstonist.com/news/ted-hsu-wins-provincial-liberal-nomination-for-kingston-and-the-islands/|access-date=February 21, 2022}}</ref> He was elected in the [[2022 Ontario general election]].

He has held the Ontario Liberal Party critic roles for the Ministry of Energy, Ministry of Natural Resources and Forestry, Ministry of Mines, and the Ministry of Citizenship and Multiculturalism. As of February 28, 2024, he serves as the Liberal Party critic for Energy and Mines, Natural Resources and Forestry, and Agricultural and Rural Issues.

Hsu was a candidate in the [[2023 Ontario Liberal Party leadership election]] but was eliminated on the first ballot when he placed fourth with 10% of the vote behind Mississauga mayor [[Bonnie Crombie]], who would win on the third ballot, runner-up [[Nathaniel Erskine-Smith]], and third-place finisher [[Yasir Naqvi]].<ref>{{cite news |date=December 2, 2023 |title=Bonnie Crombie wins Ontario Liberal leadership race, says party focused on beating Doug Ford |url=https://www.cbc.ca/news/canada/toronto/ontario-liberals-announce-new-leader-1.7047338 |access-date=December 2, 2023 |work=CBC News}}</ref>

He was handily re-elected to a second term in his riding in the [[2025 Ontario general election|2025 Ontario Provincial Election]], receiving more than 61% of the total vote, an increase of 24% compared to 2022. Hsu's margin of victory by votes was the largest in Ontario and the largest ever in his provincial riding's history. It  was also the best result for the Ontario Liberals in the 2025 election.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Ferguson |first=Elliott |date=February 27, 2025 |title=Ted Hsu wins landslide victory in Kingston and the Islands |work=thewhig |url=https://www.thewhig.com/news/ted-hsu-wins-landslide-victory-in-kingston-and-the-islands}}</ref>
